div.p: I have often thought long and hard about whether the power of speaking and the keen pursuit of eloquence have brought men and communities more good or more harm. For when I consider the losses our own commonwealth has suffered, and gather in my mind the ancient disasters of the greatest states, I see that no small part of these misfortunes was brought on by men of great eloquence; yet when I set out to recover from the records of literature those events removed from our own memory by their antiquity, I find that many cities have been founded, very many wars extinguished, the firmest alliances and the most sacred friendships formed, not only by reason of the mind but more readily by eloquence. And indeed, as I reflect long upon this, reason itself leads me above all to the view that wisdom without eloquence does communities little good, but eloquence without wisdom is most often a great harm and never a benefit. Therefore, if a man, neglecting the most upright and honourable pursuits of reason and duty, spends all his effort upon the practice of speaking, he is reared to be useless to himself and ruinous to his country; but the man who so arms himself with eloquence that he can not attack the interests of his country but defend them, he seems to me a citizen most useful and most loyal both to his own and to the public interest.

The people of Croton, when they once flourished with all manner of resources and were counted among the foremost in their prosperity in Italy, wished to enrich with outstanding pictures the temple of Juno, which they worshipped with the deepest reverence. And so they engaged at a great price Zeuxis of Heraclea, who was then thought far to excel the other painters, and brought him in. He painted many other panels, some part of which has remained even to our own memory on account of the sanctity of the shrine; and, in order that a mute image might contain in itself the surpassing beauty of the female form, he said he wished to paint a portrait of Helen. The people of Croton, who had often heard that he greatly excelled others in painting the female body, gladly heard this. For they thought that, if he had laboured greatly in the very kind in which he was most powerful, he would leave them an outstanding work in that shrine.

And if we wish to consider the origin of this thing which is called eloquence—whether it be an art, a study, a kind of practice, or a faculty derived from nature—we shall find that it sprang from the most honourable causes and proceeded from the best principles. For there was once a time when men wandered at large over the fields after the manner of beasts and sustained their lives on wild fare, doing nothing by reason of the mind but managing most things by the strength of the body. As yet no account was taken of divine religion or of human duty; no one had seen lawful marriage, no one had looked upon children certainly his own, no one had learned what advantage there was in equitable law. And so, through error and ignorance, blind and reckless desire, mistress of the mind, abused the strength of the body, those most ruinous henchmen, to satisfy itself. At this time a certain man—great, no doubt, and wise—recognized what material there was, and what great opportunity for the highest achievements lay hidden in the minds of men, if only someone could draw it out and make it better by instruction. By a certain method he gathered into one place men who were scattered over the fields and hidden away in woodland shelters, and brought them together; and leading them into every useful and honourable course of life, though at first they cried out against it because of its strangeness, then because of reason and eloquence listened with greater attention, he made them gentle and tame out of wild and savage creatures.

Nor did that expectation then deceive them. For Zeuxis at once asked them what beautiful maidens they had. But they immediately led the man to the wrestling-school and showed him many boys endowed with great beauty. For at a certain time the people of Croton far surpassed all others in bodily strength and grace, and brought home from the athletic contests the most honourable victories with the greatest praise. When, therefore, he greatly admired the forms and bodies of the boys, "The sisters of these," they said, "are maidens among us. Therefore you can guess from these what grace they have." "Then provide me, I pray," said he, "with the most beautiful of these maidens, while I paint what I have promised you, so that the truth may be transferred from a living model into a mute image."

To me at least it seems that wisdom could not have accomplished this—the sudden turning of men from their old habits and their transfer to different modes of life—if it had been silent or destitute of the power of speech. Consider further: once cities had been founded, how could it ever have come about that men learned to keep faith and to maintain justice, to obey others of their own free will, and to think it right not only to undertake labours for the common good but even to lay down their lives—unless men had been able to persuade by eloquence of what they had discovered by reason? Surely no one, when he could do most by force, would have been willing to surrender his strength to the rule of law and to put himself on a level with those whom he might have surpassed, and of his own free will to give up a most pleasant habit which by long usage had by then taken on the force of nature—unless he had been moved by weighty and agreeable speech. In this way, then, eloquence seems first to have arisen and to have advanced further, and afterwards to have been employed, with the greatest benefit to mankind, in the highest affairs of peace and war. But once a certain facility, a corrupt imitator of virtue, had attained an abundant power of speech without any regard for duty, then malice, relying on talent, grew accustomed to overthrowing cities and undermining the lives of men.

Then the people of Croton, by public decree, gathered the maidens into one place and gave the painter the power to choose whichever he wished. But he chose five, whose names many poets have handed down to memory, because they had been approved by the judgment of one who ought to have had the truest judgment of beauty. For he did not think that he could find in one body all the things he sought for loveliness, for the reason that nature has perfected nothing complete in every part in a single kind. And so, as though she would not have anything left to bestow on the rest if she granted everything to one, she endows each with some advantage joined to some defect.

And since I have spoken of the beginning of this good, let me explain the origin of this evil too. It seems to me most probable that there was a time when men inarticulate and unwise were not in the habit of taking part in public affairs, nor did great and eloquent men come forward to plead private cases; but while the most important matters were administered by the most eminent men, I suppose there were others, not without cleverness, who took up the petty disputes of private persons. In these disputes, since men often grew accustomed to standing for falsehood against the truth, constant practice in speaking bred audacity, so that of necessity those better men were compelled, on account of the wrongs done to their fellow citizens, to resist the bold, and each to bring help to his own connections. And so, since in speaking the man who, abandoning the pursuit of wisdom, had acquired nothing for himself but eloquence often seemed an equal and sometimes even a superior, it came about that, in the judgment both of the multitude and of himself, he was thought worthy to govern the state. From this it followed, not unjustly, that when rash and audacious men had come to the helm of the commonwealth, the greatest and most miserable shipwrecks occurred. By these things eloquence drew upon itself so much hatred and ill will that the most gifted men, as though escaping from some violent storm into harbour, withdrew from the seditious and turbulent life into some quiet pursuit. And so it seems to me that afterwards the other upright and honourable studies, cultivated in leisure by the best men, shone forth, while this one was abandoned by most of them and fell into disuse at the very time when it ought to have been retained far more firmly and increased more zealously.

Now since it has fallen to us too, by our wish, to write out an art of speaking, we have not set before ourselves any single model, all the parts of which, in whatever kind they were, we should think it necessary for us to express; but, having gathered all the writers into one place, we have excerpted from each what each seemed to teach most fittingly, and have gleaned the most excellent things from various talents. For of those who are worthy of name and memory, no one seemed to us to say nothing in the best manner, nor everything most excellently. Therefore it seemed folly either to withdraw from someone's good discoveries, if we were offended by some fault of his, or to add ourselves to the faults of one too by whose good precept we were guided in something.

For the more unworthily the rashness and audacity of foolish and wicked men violated a thing most honourable and most upright, to the greatest detriment of the commonwealth, the more zealously should those men have been resisted and the commonwealth looked to. This did not escape our own Cato, nor Laelius, nor—to speak truly—their disciple Africanus, nor the Gracchi, grandsons of Africanus; in these men there was the highest virtue, and authority enlarged by the highest virtue, and eloquence, which was both an ornament to these qualities and a safeguard to the commonwealth. Therefore in my own judgment eloquence ought to be pursued no less, even though certain men abuse it both in private and in public; rather, it ought to be pursued the more vigorously, lest the wicked should have very great power, to the great detriment of the good and the common ruin of all—especially since this is the one thing which most of all bears upon every matter, private and public alike, by which life is made safe, honourable, distinguished, and at the same time pleasant. For from this very great benefits come to the commonwealth, if wisdom, the guide of all things, is at hand; from this come praise, honour, and dignity to the men who have attained it; from this too the surest and safest protection is provided for their friends. And to me indeed it seems that men, though in many respects lowlier and weaker than the beasts, surpass them above all in this, that they can speak. Therefore it seems to me a splendid thing for a man to have attained excellence over other men in the very respect in which men surpass the beasts. And since this is brought about not by nature and practice alone, but is also acquired by a certain art, it is not out of place to see what those men say who have left us some precepts on the subject. But before we speak of the rules of oratory, it seems right to speak of the nature of the art itself, of its function, its end, its material, and its parts. For once these things are known, the mind of each man will be able more easily and readily to consider the very method and course of the art.

But if in the other pursuits too men preferred to choose from many the most fitting thing rather than to attach themselves certainly to some one person, they would offend less in arrogance; they would not persevere so greatly in faults; they would suffer somewhat more lightly from ignorance. And if our knowledge of this art had been equal to his of painting, perhaps this work of ours would shine forth in its kind more than that noble picture of his in its own. For the power of choosing among examples was greater for us than for him. He was able to choose from one city and from that number of maidens who then existed; but to us, with the resources displayed of all who have existed from the very beginning of this instruction down to this time, there was the power of choosing whatever we pleased.

There is a certain science of civic life which consists of many great matters. A great and ample part of it is artful eloquence, which they call rhetoric. For we do not agree with those who think that political science has no need of eloquence, and we strongly disagree with those who think it is wholly contained in the power and art of the rhetorician. Therefore we shall place this oratorical faculty in such a class as to say that it is a part of political science. The function of this faculty seems to be to speak in a manner suited to producing persuasion; its end is to persuade by speech. Between function and end there is this difference, that in the function we consider what ought to be done, in the end what ought to be effected. As we say that the function of the physician is to treat in a manner suited to healing, and his end to heal by treatment, so too we understand what we should call the function and what the end of the orator when we say that what he ought to do is his function, and that for the sake of which he ought to do it we call his end.

And indeed Aristotle gathered into one place the ancient writers on the art, traced back even to that prince and inventor Tisias, and, with great care, sought out by name the precepts of each, set them down clearly, and expounded them carefully and distinctly; and he so surpassed the inventors themselves in agreeableness and brevity of speech, that no one learns their precepts from their own books, but all who wish to understand what those men teach return to him as to a much more convenient expositor.

We call the material of an art that with which the whole art and the faculty produced by the art is concerned. As if we should say that the material of medicine is diseases and wounds, because all medicine is concerned with these, so the matters with which the art and faculty of oratory is concerned we name the material of the art of rhetoric. Some have reckoned these matters more, others fewer. For Gorgias of Leontini, almost the earliest rhetorician, held that the orator could speak best on all subjects whatever; he seems to assign to this art an unlimited and boundless material. Aristotle, however, who furnished this art with very many aids and ornaments, held that the function of the rhetorician was concerned with three classes of subjects: the demonstrative, the deliberative, and the judicial. The demonstrative is that which is devoted to the praise or blame of some particular person; the deliberative, which, set in political debate, involves the expression of an opinion; the judicial, which, set in a court of law, involves accusation and defence, or claim and rejection. And, as our own opinion holds, the art and faculty of the orator is to be regarded as concerned with this threefold material.

And he himself, indeed, set both himself and those who had been before him before us in plain view, so that we might come to know both the others and himself through himself; and those who set out from him, although they spent very much of their labour on the greatest parts of philosophy, just as he himself, whose principles they followed, had done, nevertheless left us very many precepts of speaking. And other teachers of speaking too flowed forth from another source, who likewise greatly assisted toward speaking, if the art accomplishes anything. For at the same time as Aristotle there was a great and noble rhetorician, Isocrates;

For Hermagoras certainly seems neither to attend to what he says nor to understand what he promises, when he divides the orator's material into "cause" and "question," and says that a cause is a matter which involves a controversy set in speech, with the introduction of definite persons—which we too say is assigned to the orator (for we place under it the three parts we mentioned before: the judicial, the deliberative, the demonstrative). But he calls a "question" that which involves a controversy set in speech without the introduction of definite persons, of this kind: Is there any good besides the honourable? Are the senses trustworthy? What is the shape of the universe? What is the size of the sun? Such questions everyone, I think, readily understands to be far removed from the orator's function; for to assign to the orator, as though they were some trifling matters, those questions on which we know the highest talents of the philosophers have been spent with the greatest labour, seems great madness. But if Hermagoras had possessed in these matters a great faculty acquired by study and training, he would seem, relying on his own knowledge, to have laid down something false about the orator's art, and to have set forth not what the art can do but what he himself could do. As it is, the man's power is such that one would sooner take rhetoric from him than grant him philosophy—not that I think the art he published was written by him most faultily; for in it he seems to have collected and arranged matters chosen with ingenuity and care from the ancient treatises, and to have contributed something new himself. But it is of very little importance to the orator to talk about the art, which is what he did, and of the very greatest importance to speak by the art, which we all see he was least able to do.

of whose own work we have not found what art is agreed to be his. But of his pupils, and of those who set out directly from this school, we have found many precepts on the art. From these two distinct families, as it were—of which the one, while it was engaged in philosophy, took upon itself some care for the art of rhetoric too, while the other was wholly occupied in the study and teaching of speaking—a certain single kind was fused together by later men, who brought into their own treatises, from both, those things which seemed fitly said; and these very men, together with those earlier ones, we have set before ourselves, all of them, as far as our ability allowed, and have ourselves too contributed something to the common store.

The material, then, of the art of rhetoric seems to us to be that which we have said seemed so to Aristotle; and its parts are those which most authorities have named: invention, arrangement, expression, memory, and delivery. Invention is the devising of matters true or probable, which may render a cause persuasive; arrangement is the distribution of the matters discovered into their proper order; expression is the fitting of suitable words to the matter discovered; memory is the firm grasp by the mind of the matters and words belonging to the invention; delivery is the regulation of voice and body in keeping with the dignity of the matters and words. Now, having briefly settled these things, we shall put off to another time those discussions by which we might show the nature, end, and function of this art; for they require many words and do not so greatly pertain to the description of the art and the handing down of its rules. But we hold that one who writes a treatise on the art of rhetoric ought to write about the two remaining matters, the material of the art and its parts. And to me indeed it seems that the material and the parts should be treated together. Therefore let invention, which is the chief of all the parts, be considered above all, in every kind of cause—what it ought to be.

But if those things which are set forth in these books had to be chosen with as much care as the zeal with which they have been chosen, surely neither we nor others will regret our diligence. But if we shall seem rashly to have passed over something of someone's, or to have followed something not elegantly enough, we shall easily and gladly change our opinion when taught by someone. For it is not disgraceful to have learned too little, but to have persevered foolishly and long in what one has learned too little; for the one is attributed to the common weakness of men,

Every matter which involves some controversy set in speech and debate contains a question either of fact, or of name, or of kind, or of procedure. This question, then, from which the cause arises, we call the "issue." The issue is the first clash of the cases, arising from the rejection of the charge, in this manner: "You did it"—"I did not do it," or "I did it lawfully." When there is a controversy of fact, since the case is established by conjectures, the issue is called conjectural. When there is a controversy of name, since the meaning of the term must be defined in words, the issue is called definitional. When the question is what kind of thing the matter is, since the controversy concerns both the nature and the kind of the act, the issue is called general (qualitative). But when the case turns on this, that either the wrong person seems to be conducting the action, or not against the person he should, or not before the proper persons, or not at the proper time, or under the proper law, on the proper charge, with the proper penalty, the issue is called translative, because the action seems to need transfer and change. And one of these must fall upon every kind of cause; for in any matter upon which it does not fall, there can be no controversy. Therefore it is not even fit to be considered a cause.

the other to the particular fault of each. Therefore we, for our part, without any positive assertion, while at the same time inquiring, shall state each thing tentatively, lest, while we gain some trifle—that we should seem to have written these things out fitly enough—we lose that which is greatest, namely, that we should not have assented to anything rashly and arrogantly. But this indeed we shall zealously aim at, both at this time and throughout our whole life, as far as our ability will allow; now, however, lest our discourse seem to have advanced too far, we shall speak of the rest of the things which seem to need teaching.

A controversy of fact can be assigned to all the tenses. For one can inquire what has been done, in this manner: Did Ulysses kill Ajax? and what is being done, in this manner: Are the people of Fregellae well disposed toward the Roman people? and what will be done, in this manner: If we leave Carthage unharmed, will any harm come to the commonwealth? There is a controversy of name when there is agreement about the fact, and the question is by what name that which was done should be called. In this class there must necessarily be a controversy of name because there is disagreement about the matter itself—not because the fact is in doubt, but because what was done seems one thing to one person and another to another, and therefore each calls it by a different name. Therefore in cases of this kind the matter must be defined in words and briefly described, as, for instance, if someone has stolen a sacred object from a private place, whether he is to be judged a thief or a temple-robber; for when this is in question, it will be necessary to define both, what a thief is and what a temple-robber is, and by one's own description to show that the matter under discussion ought to be called by another name than that which our opponents use.

The first book, then, having set forth the nature of this art and its function, end, material, and parts, contained the kinds of controversies, the methods of invention, and the issues; then the parts of the speech, and into all of these all the precepts. Therefore, since in it the other matters were stated more distinctly, but those concerning confirmation and refutation in a scattered way, now we think we should hand down definite topics of confirming and refuting for each several kind of cause. And because it was set forth not carelessly in the first book in what way arguments ought to be handled, here only the discovered matters themselves will be set forth for each thing simply, without any embellishment, so that from this the discoveries themselves, but from the earlier book the polishing of the discoveries, may be sought. Therefore these things which will now be taught must be referred to the parts of confirmation and refutation.

There is a controversy of kind when it is agreed what has been done, and it is settled by what name what was done ought to be called, and yet the question is how great, of what character, and in general of what quality it is, in this manner: is it just or unjust, useful or useless, and all those questions in which the inquiry is what quality belongs to the thing that was done, without any controversy of name. To this class Hermagoras assigned four subdivisions: the deliberative, the demonstrative, the juridical, and the negotial. This error of his—no slight one, as we think—seems to deserve censure, but briefly, lest, if we pass it over in silence, we be thought to have failed to follow him without reason, or, if we dwell upon it too long, we be thought to have introduced delay and hindrance into the rest of our precepts. If deliberation and demonstration are kinds of causes, they cannot rightly be considered parts of some kind of cause; for the same thing can be a kind to one person and a part to another, but it cannot be a kind and a part of the same thing. But deliberation and demonstration are kinds of causes. For either there is no kind of cause at all, or only the judicial, or the judicial and the demonstrative and the deliberative. To say there is no kind of cause, when he says there are many causes and gives precepts for them, is madness; but how can the judicial alone exist, when deliberation and demonstration are neither alike to each other nor like the judicial kind, but differ from it very greatly, and each has its own end to which it ought to be referred? It remains, then, that there are three kinds of causes.

Every demonstrative, deliberative, and judicial cause must necessarily turn on some one or more of those kinds of issue which were set forth before. Although this is so, nevertheless, while certain things can be taught in common about all, separately too there are different instructions for each kind. For praise ought to accomplish one thing, blame another, the expression of an opinion another, accusation or defence another. In trials it is inquired what is just; in demonstrations, what is honourable; in deliberations, as we hold, both what is honourable and what is useful. For the others have thought that in advising and dissuading the end ought to be set forth only in terms of usefulness.

But if the parts of a kind of cause cannot rightly be so considered, much less rightly will the parts of a part of a cause be so considered. Now every issue is a part of a cause; for the cause is not fitted to the issue, but the issue to the cause. But demonstration and deliberation cannot rightly be considered parts of a kind of cause, because they are themselves kinds; much less rightly, then, will they be considered parts of that thing which is here called a part. Again, if the issue itself and any part of it is a rejection of the charge, then whatever is not a rejection of the charge is neither an issue nor a part of an issue; deliberation and demonstration are neither an issue nor a part of an issue. But he himself holds that the issue is a rejection of the charge; he must therefore hold that demonstration and deliberation are neither an issue nor a part of an issue. And he will be pressed by this same argument whether he calls the issue the first confirmation of the accuser's case or the first plea of the defendant's; for all the same difficulties will follow him.

Of those kinds, then, whose ends and outcomes are different, the precepts cannot be the same. Nor do we now say this, that the same issues do not fall upon them; but nevertheless a certain kind of speech arises from the very end and from the kind of cause, which pertains to the demonstration of someone's life or to the expression of an opinion. Therefore we shall now be occupied with the judicial kind of causes and of precepts, from which most things are transferred to the other kinds of causes too, when a similar controversy is involved, without any difficulty; afterwards we shall speak separately about the rest.

Again, a conjectural cause cannot at the same time, in the same respect and the same kind, be both conjectural and definitional. Nor can a definitional cause at the same time, in the same respect and the same kind, be both definitional and translative. And in general no issue or part of an issue can at once contain both its own force and that of another within it, because each one is considered in itself and by its own nature simply; when a second is added, the number of issues is doubled, but the force of the issue is not increased. But a deliberative cause is wont, at the same time, in the same respect and the same kind, to have a conjectural, a general, a definitional, and a translative issue—one, or sometimes several. Therefore it is itself neither an issue nor a part of an issue. The same is wont to happen in demonstration. These, then, as we said before, are to be considered kinds of causes, not parts of any issue. This issue, then, which we call general, seems to us to have two parts, the juridical and the negotial. The juridical is that in which the nature of equity and right, or the principle of reward or punishment, is inquired into; the negotial is that in which it is considered what is lawful according to civil custom and equity;

Now let us begin from the conjectural issue, of which let this be the example set forth: on a journey, someone accompanied a man who was setting out for a certain market and was carrying with him a fair sum of money. He fell into conversation with him, as commonly happens, on the road; from which it came about that they wished to make that journey more companionably. Therefore, when they had turned aside into the same inn, they wished to dine together and to take their rest in the same place. Having dined, they lay down to sleep in the same place. But the innkeeper—for so he is called after he was discovered, when he was caught in another crime—when he had noticed that other man, namely the one who had the money, by night, after he perceived that they were already sleeping rather soundly from weariness, came up and drew from its sheath the sword of the other of them, the one who was without money, which lay near at hand, and killed that other man, took away the money, put the bloody sword back in its sheath, and betook himself to his own bed. But that man by whose sword the killing had been done arose long before dawn, called to his companion once and again.

and the men we call jurists are thought to preside over this kind of inquiry among us. And the juridical itself is divided into two parts, the absolute and the assumptive. The absolute is that which contains in itself the question of right and wrong; the assumptive is that which of itself supplies nothing firm for the defence, but borrows from outside some support for the case. Its parts are four: confession (concession), shifting of the charge, retort of the charge, and comparison. Concession is when the defendant does not defend what was done, but begs to be pardoned. This is divided into two parts: purgation and entreaty. Purgation is when the act is admitted, but the guilt is removed. This has three parts: ignorance, accident, and necessity. Entreaty is when the defendant confesses that he has done wrong, and done wrong deliberately, and yet begs to be pardoned; a kind of plea which can very rarely occur. The shifting of the charge is when the defendant tries to remove from himself and from his own fault and power onto another the charge brought against him. This can be done in two ways: if either the cause or the act is transferred to another. The cause is transferred when it is said to have been done by another's force and power; the act, when another is said to have had the duty or the power to do it. The retort of the charge is when the act is said to have been done lawfully because someone first provoked it by a wrong. Comparison is when it is maintained that some other act, right or useful, was the reason for which the one charged is said to have been committed.

He thought the man, hindered by sleep, was not answering; he took up his sword and the rest of the things he had brought with him, and set out alone. Not long after, the innkeeper raised the cry that a man had been murdered, and, with some of the lodgers, overtook on the road the man who had gone out earlier. He seized the man, drew his sword from its sheath, and found it bloody. The man was led back to the city by them and became the accused. In this case the charge is: "You killed him." The rebuttal: "I did not kill him." From these the issue is the same as the point for decision: "Did he kill him?"

In the fourth issue, which we call translative, there is a controversy of that issue when the question is who, or against whom, or in what manner, or before whom, or by what right, or at what time one ought to bring an action, or when in general some change or invalidation of the action is at stake. Hermagoras is thought to be the discoverer of this issue—not because earlier orators did not often make use of it, but because the writers on the art before him did not notice it nor count it among the issues. But after it had been discovered by him, many found fault with it; and these, I think, are hindered not so much by ignorance (for the matter is plain) as by envy and a certain disposition to disparage. And so we have set forth both the issues and their parts; but examples of each kind we shall set forth more conveniently when we provide an abundance of arguments for each of them; for the method of arguing will be clearer when it can at once be fitted both to the kind and to an example of a cause.

Now we shall set forth the topics, some part of which falls upon every conjectural controversy. But in setting forth these topics and the rest, it will be necessary to attend to this: that not all suit every cause. For just as every name is written from some, not from all, the letters, so not the whole abundance of arguments, but necessarily some part of them, will suit every cause. Every conjecture, then, is to be taken from the cause, from the person, and from the deed itself.

Once the issue of the cause has been found, it is well at once to consider whether the cause is simple or compound; and if it is compound, whether it is compounded of several questions or of some comparison. It is simple when it contains in itself one absolute question, in this manner: Shall we declare war on the Corinthians, or not? It is compounded of several questions when more things than one are inquired into, in this manner: Shall Carthage be destroyed, or restored to the Carthaginians, or shall a colony be settled there? It involves comparison when, by way of contrast, the question is which is preferable, or what is most expedient, in this manner: Shall an army be sent into Macedonia against Philip, to bring aid to our allies, or shall it be kept in Italy, so that the greatest possible forces may be at hand against Hannibal? Next we must consider whether the controversy is one of reasoning or of writing; for a controversy of writing is that which arises from the character of a written document. Its kinds, which are distinct from the issues, are five. For sometimes the words themselves seem to be at variance with the writer's intention; sometimes two or more laws are at variance with one another; sometimes what is written seems to signify two or more things; sometimes from what is written something else is inferred which is not written; sometimes the meaning of a word is in question, as in the definitional issue—in what it consists. Therefore we name the first kind "from the letter and the intent," the second "from contrary laws," the third "ambiguity," the fourth "inference (ratiocinative)," the fifth "definitional."

The cause is divided into impulse and reasoning. Impulse is that which urges one to do something without reflection, through some disposition of the mind, such as love, anger, distress, drunkenness, and in general all those things in which the mind seems to have been so disposed that it could not perceive the matter with deliberation and care, and did what it did rather by a kind of impulse of the mind than by reflection.

But the controversy is one of reasoning when the whole question rests not on a written text but on some process of argument. And so, when you have considered the kind of cause—when you have understood whether it is simple or compound, and have seen whether it has a controversy of writing or of reasoning—you must next see what the question, the reason, the point for decision, and the foundation of the cause are; all of which must proceed from the issue. The question is that controversy which is generated by the clash of the cases, in this manner: "You did not act lawfully"—"I acted lawfully." Now the clash of the cases is that in which the issue consists. From it, then, arises the controversy which we call the question, namely: Did he act lawfully? The reason is that which contains the cause, and which, if it were taken away, would leave no controversy in the cause—in this manner, to take, for the sake of instruction, an easy and familiar example: if Orestes were accused of matricide, unless he should say "I acted lawfully, for she had killed my father," he has no defence; and once this reason is taken away, the whole controversy is taken away too. The reason of his case, then, is that she had killed Agamemnon. The point for decision is the controversy which arises from the invalidation of the reason. For let the reason which we set forth a little before be put before us: "for she," he says, "had killed my father"; "but," the opponent will say, "it was not right for the mother to be slain by you, her son; for her deed could have been punished without crime on your part." From this rebuttal of the reason arises that crowning controversy which we call the point for decision. It is of this kind: Was it right for Orestes to kill his mother, since she had killed his father?

Reasoning, however, is the careful and considered devising of doing or not doing something. It is said to have been at work when the mind seems to have avoided or pursued something for a definite reason: if something is said to have been done for the sake of friendship, or of avenging an enemy, or out of fear, or for glory, or for money, or, finally—to embrace everything by kind—for the sake of retaining, increasing, or obtaining some advantage, or, on the contrary, of rejecting, diminishing, or avoiding some disadvantage. For under one or the other of these kinds will fall also those cases in which either some lesser disadvantage is undertaken for the sake of obtaining a greater advantage or avoiding a greater disadvantage, or some advantage is passed over for the sake of obtaining a greater advantage or avoiding a greater disadvantage.

The foundation is the firmest argument of the defender, and the most fitted to the point for decision: as if Orestes should wish to say that his mother's disposition toward his father, toward himself and his sisters, toward the kingdom, and toward the reputation of their race and family was such that her own children above all had a duty to exact punishment from her. And in the other issues, indeed, the points for decision are found in this way; but in the conjectural issue, because there is no reason—for the fact is not admitted—the point for decision cannot arise from the rebuttal of a reason. Therefore the question and the point for decision must be the same: "It was done"—"It was not done"—"Was it done?" And however many issues or parts of issues there are in a cause, so many questions, reasons, points for decision, and foundations must be found. Then, once all these have been found in the cause, the several parts of the whole cause must finally be considered. For it is not the case that whatever is to be said first should also be attended to first; the reason being that those things which are said first, if you wish them strongly to agree and cohere with the cause, must be drawn from those which are to be said later. Therefore, when the point for decision, and the arguments which ought to be found bearing on the point for decision, have been carefully discovered by art and thoroughly worked over by care and thought, then at last the other parts of the speech are to be arranged. These parts seem to us to be six in all: the exordium, the narrative, the partition, the confirmation, the refutation, and the conclusion. Now, since the exordium ought to be first, we too shall first give precepts on the method of beginning.

This topic is, as it were, a kind of foundation of this issue. For it is proved to no one that anything was done, unless something is shown as the reason why it was done. Therefore the accuser, when he says that something was done by impulse, will have to amplify with words and reflections that impulse and a certain agitation and disposition of mind, and to show how great is the force of love, how great a disturbance of mind arises from anger or from some one of those causes by which he will say that someone, impelled, did the deed. Here, both by the mention of examples of those who under a like impulse have committed some deed, and by the comparison of similarities, and by the explanation of the very disposition of mind, care must be taken that it may not seem surprising if a mind moved by such a disturbance has gone forward to some crime.

The exordium is a passage which suitably prepares the hearer's mind for the rest of the speech: which will happen if it has rendered him well-disposed, attentive, and receptive. Therefore, whoever wishes to make a good beginning to his cause must first carefully understand the kind of his cause. There are five kinds of causes: the honourable, the surprising (discreditable), the lowly, the doubtful, and the obscure. The honourable kind of cause is that to which the hearer's mind is favourable at once, without any speech of ours; the surprising is that from which the minds of those who are to hear are alienated; the lowly is that which is disregarded by the hearer and seems to deserve no great attention; the doubtful is that in which either the point for decision is uncertain, or the cause partakes both of honour and of baseness, so that it gives rise both to good will and to offence; the obscure is that in which either the hearers are dull or the cause is involved in matters too difficult to understand. Therefore, since the kinds of causes are so different, it is necessary to begin in a different way in each kind. The exordium, then, is divided into two parts, the introduction (direct opening) and the insinuation (subtle approach). The introduction is a passage which clearly and at once renders the hearer well-disposed, or receptive, or attentive. The insinuation is a passage which, by a certain dissimulation and circuitous approach, secretly steals into the hearer's mind.

But when he says that someone committed something not by impulse but by reasoning, he will demonstrate what advantage he pursued or what disadvantage he fled, and will magnify this as much as he can, so that, so far as may be, the cause that urged him to wrongdoing may seem as adequate as possible. If for the sake of glory, how great a glory he thought he would obtain; likewise if for the sake of dominion, of money, of friendship, of enmity, and in general whatever there is that he says was the cause, he will have to magnify it to the utmost.

In the surprising kind of cause, if the hearers are not altogether hostile, it will be possible to gain their good will by an introduction. But if they are strongly alienated, it will be necessary to resort to insinuation. For if peace and good will are openly sought from men who are angry, not only are they not obtained, but the hatred is increased and inflamed. In the lowly kind of cause, however, in order to remove contempt, it is necessary to make the hearer attentive. If the doubtful kind of cause has an uncertain point for decision, one must begin from the point for decision itself. But if it partakes partly of baseness and partly of honour, it will be fitting to capture good will, so that the cause may seem to be transferred into the honourable kind. But when the cause is of the honourable kind, the introduction may either be omitted, or, if it is convenient, we may begin from the narrative, or from a law, or from some very firm argument of our own speech; or if we choose to use an introduction, we must employ the means of producing good will, so that what already exists may be increased. In the obscure kind of cause we must by the introduction make the hearers receptive. Now, since it has been stated what things the exordium ought to accomplish, it remains to show by what methods each of them may be accomplished.

And he will have to consider this carefully: not only what existed in truth, but even more emphatically what existed in the opinion of the one he accuses. For it matters nothing that some advantage or disadvantage did not or does not exist, if it can be shown that it seemed so to the one accused. For opinion deceives men in two ways, when either the matter is otherwise than it is thought, or the outcome is not what they supposed. The matter is otherwise when men either think that good which is evil, or, on the contrary, that evil which is good, or think that which is neither evil nor good to be evil or good, or that which is evil or good to be neither evil nor good.

Good will is procured from four sources: from our own person, from that of our opponents, from that of the judges, and from the cause. From our own person, if we speak of our deeds and services without arrogance; if we dispel the charges brought against us and any less than honourable suspicions cast upon us; if we set forth the misfortunes that have befallen us or the difficulties that threaten us; if we make use of prayer and humble, suppliant entreaty. From the person of our opponents, if we bring them into hatred, or envy, or contempt. They will be brought into hatred if some foul, arrogant, cruel, or malicious deed of theirs is set forth; into envy, if their power, influence, wealth, and connections are set forth, and their arrogant and intolerable use of these, so that they seem to rely on these things rather than on their cause; into contempt, if their idleness, negligence, sloth, lazy pursuits, and luxurious leisure are set forth. From the person of the hearers good will will be captured, if their brave, wise, and gentle deeds are set forth, so that no excessive flattery is shown, and if it is pointed out how honourable is the esteem in which they are held, and how great the expectation of their judgment and authority; from the cause, if we exalt our own case by praising it, and depress our opponents' case through contempt.

With this understood, if anyone shall deny that any money is dearer or sweeter than the life of a brother or friend, or finally than duty, this the accuser will not have to deny. For the fault and the greatest hatred will be transferred to him who denies what is said so truly and dutifully. But this must be said, that it did not seem so to that man;

We shall make the hearers attentive if we show that the matters we are about to speak of are great, novel, and incredible, or that they pertain either to all men, or to those who are listening, or to certain distinguished men, or to the immortal gods, or to the highest interest of the commonwealth; and if we promise that we shall briefly demonstrate our case, and set forth the point for decision, or the points for decision, if there are several. We shall make the hearers receptive if we set forth openly and briefly the substance of the cause, that is, the point on which the controversy turns. For when you wish to make a hearer receptive, you must at the same time make him attentive; for the man who is most ready to listen most attentively is the most receptive. Now it seems we must next speak of how insinuations are properly handled. Insinuation, then, is to be used when the kind of cause is surprising—that is, as we said before, when the hearer's mind is hostile. This comes about chiefly from three causes: either there is some baseness in the cause itself, or something seems already to have been impressed upon the hearer by those who spoke before, or the opportunity to speak is given at a time when those who ought to listen are already worn out with listening. For from this last circumstance too, no less than from the first two, the hearer's mind is sometimes turned against the orator.

which must be taken from those things which pertain to the person, about which we must speak later. The outcome, again, deceives when it falls out otherwise than those who are accused are said to have supposed: as if someone is said to have killed another than he wished, because he was deceived either by a resemblance, or by suspicion, or by a false demonstration; or to have killed one by whose will he is not the heir, because he thought himself heir by that will. For one ought not to regard the design by the outcome, but to consider with what design and hope the mind set out to the crime; with what intent each man does anything, not what chance he meets with, is what pertains to the matter.

If baseness in the cause produces offence, one must either substitute, for the man at whom offence is taken, another man who is liked; or for the matter at which offence is taken, another matter which is approved; or a man for a matter, or a matter for a man, so that the hearer's mind may be drawn from what it hates to what it likes; and you must conceal that you are going to defend what you are believed to be defending; then, when the hearer has now become milder, you must enter step by step upon the defence, and say that what your opponents think outrageous seems outrageous to you also; then, when you have softened the listener, you must show that none of these things concerns you, and deny that you will say anything about your opponents, neither this nor that, so as neither openly to wound those who are liked, and yet, doing this covertly, to alienate the hearers' good will from them as far as you can; and you must bring forward the judgment or authority of certain men in a similar matter, worthy of imitation; then show that the same, or a like, or a greater, or a lesser matter is at issue in the present case.

Now on this topic the chief point for the accuser will be if he can show that no one else had a cause for doing it; the secondary, if no one else had so great or so fitting a cause. But if it shall seem that others too had a cause for doing it, it must be demonstrated that others lacked either the power, or the means, or the will. The power, if they shall be said either not to have known, or not to have been present, or not to have been able to accomplish anything. The means, if it shall be demonstrated that the method, the helpers, the aids, and the rest which pertained to the matter were lacking to someone. The will, if the mind shall be said to have been free and clear of such deeds. Finally, the arguments which we shall give to the accused for his defence, the accuser will turn to use in clearing others of fault. But this must be done briefly, and many things must be drawn together into one, so that he may seem not to be accusing this man for the sake of defending another, but to be defending another for the sake of accusing this man.

But if the speech of your opponents seems to have won the belief of the hearers—which will be easy to recognize for one who understands by what means belief is produced—you ought either to promise that you will speak first about that point which your opponents thought their strongest and which the hearers approved most, or to begin from the opponent's statement, and especially from what he said most recently, or to make use of hesitation, with an air of astonishment, as to what to say first or to which point above all you should reply. For when the hearer sees that the man whom he thought confounded by the opponents' speech is ready to speak against them with a most steadfast spirit, he generally judges that he himself rather assented rashly than that the other is confident without cause. But if weariness has alienated the hearer's interest from the cause, it is well to promise that you will speak more briefly than you had prepared to do, and that you will not imitate your opponent. If the matter allows, it is not useless to begin with something novel or amusing, either something arising on the spur of the moment—such as some noise or shout—or something already prepared, which contains an apologue, or a fable, or some piece of ridicule; or, if the dignity of the matter takes away the opportunity for jesting, it is not amiss to throw in at once something sad, novel, or terrible. For just as satiety and disgust at food are relieved by something rather bitter or softened by something sweet, so the mind, wearied with listening, is restored by astonishment or renewed by laughter. And these, in general, are the things which seemed worth saying separately about the introduction and the insinuation; now it seems right to give briefly one precept common to both. The exordium ought to have very much of weighty thought and of dignity, and to contain in itself all those things which pertain to dignity; for this reason, that what most commends the orator to the hearer ought to be done best of all. It ought to have very little of brilliance, gaiety, and elaborate neatness; for from these arises a certain suspicion of contrivance and artificial pains, which most of all takes away credit from the speech and authority from the orator.

And these, in general, are the things the accuser must consider. But the defender, on the contrary, will first say either that there was no impulse, or, if he shall grant that there was, will diminish it and demonstrate that it was some slight one, or will teach that such deeds are not wont to arise from it. On which topic it must be demonstrated what is the force and nature of that disposition by which the accused is said, impelled, to have committed something; in which both examples and similarities must be brought forward, and the very nature of that disposition must be carefully explained on its mildest and quietest side, so that both the matter itself may be drawn from a cruel and turbulent deed to something gentler and more tranquil, and the speech nevertheless may be adapted to the mind of him who hears, and to a certain inmost feeling of the mind.

These are the surest faults of exordia, which it will be necessary to take the greatest care to avoid: the commonplace, the interchangeable, the convertible, the long, the detached, the transferable, and that which is contrary to the precepts. The commonplace is that which can be fitted to several causes, so as to seem appropriate. The interchangeable is that which can equally well suit this side of a cause and its opposite. The convertible is that which can, with slight alteration, be used by the opponent for the contrary side. The long is that which is drawn out with more words or thoughts than is enough. The detached is that which is not drawn from the cause itself, nor attached to the speech like some member of the body. The transferable is that which accomplishes something other than the kind of cause demands: as if one should make the hearer receptive when the cause requires good will, or use an introduction when the matter requires insinuation. That which is contrary to the precepts is that which accomplishes none of the things for the sake of which the precepts about exordia are handed down; that is, which renders the hearer neither well-disposed, nor attentive, nor receptive, or—than which surely nothing is worse—does the opposite. And about the exordium enough has now been said.

But he will weaken the suspicions of reasoning if he shall say either that there was no advantage, or a small one, or one greater for others, or none greater for himself than for others, or a disadvantage greater for himself than the advantage, so that by no means was the magnitude of that advantage which is said to have been sought to be compared either with that disadvantage which would have followed, or with that danger which would be undergone;

The narrative is the setting forth of things done, or as though done. There are three kinds of narrative. One kind is that in which the cause itself and the whole basis of the controversy is contained; another, in which some digression beyond the cause is introduced, for the sake of disparagement, or comparison, or amusement not foreign to the matter under discussion, or amplification. The third kind is removed from civil causes, and is spoken and written for the sake of amusement, together with not unprofitable practice. Of this last there are two parts, one of which is concerned chiefly with matters, the other with persons. That which is set in the exposition of matters has three parts: the legend, history, and the realistic plot. A legend is that in which things neither true nor probable are contained, of this kind: "Huge winged serpents, yoked to a chariot . . ." History is an event done, removed from the memory of our own age; of this kind: "Appius declared war upon the Carthaginians." A realistic plot is a fictitious matter which nevertheless could have happened—of this kind, in Terence: "For after he had passed out of boyhood . . ." But that narrative which is concerned with persons is of such a kind that in it, together with the matters themselves, the conversations and the dispositions of the persons can be perceived, in this manner: "He came to me often, crying: 'What are you doing, Micio? Why are you ruining the young man for us? Why does he love? Why does he drink? Why do you supply the means for these things, and indulge him in excessive finery? You are too foolish.' He himself is too harsh, beyond what is fair and good." In this kind of narrative there ought to be much liveliness, made up of variety of matters, diversity of dispositions, gravity, gentleness, hope, fear, suspicion, longing, dissimulation, error, pity, the reversals of fortune, unexpected misfortune, sudden joy, and a pleasant outcome of events. But these ornaments will be taken from the precepts which will later be given about expression.

all of which topics will be handled in like manner in the avoidance of a disadvantage too. But if the accuser shall say that he pursued what seemed to him an advantage, or fled what he thought a disadvantage, although he was in a false opinion, it must be demonstrated by the defender that no one is of such folly as to be able, in such a matter, to be ignorant of the truth. But if this be granted, that other point will not be granted: that he did not even hesitate as to what was the right in the matter, and approved as true, without any hesitation, what was false; because if he hesitated, it was the greatest madness, impelled by a doubtful hope, to commit himself to a certain danger.

Now it seems we must speak of the narrative which contains the exposition of the cause. It ought, then, to have three qualities: that it be brief, that it be clear, and that it be plausible. It will be brief if the beginning is taken from the point where it is necessary, and is not fetched from the very first; and if, where it is enough to have stated the sum of a matter, the details of it are not stated—for often it is enough to say what was done, so that you need not narrate how it was done; and if the narration does not proceed further than is needful; and if you do not pass off into any other matter; and if it is so told that sometimes, from what has been said, what has not been said may be understood; and if not only what is harmful, but even what is neither harmful nor helpful, is passed over; and if each single thing is said once; and if the narration does not begin again from the point at which it last left off. And the imitation of brevity deceives many, so that, while they think themselves brief, they are exceedingly long, since they take pains to say many things briefly, not to say altogether few things and no more than necessary. For to most people that man seems to speak briefly who speaks thus: "I came up to the house. I called the slave. He answered. I asked for his master. He said he was not at home." Here, although he could not have stated so many things more briefly, yet, because it was enough to have said "He said he was not at home," he becomes long by the multitude of matters. Therefore in this kind too the imitation of brevity must be avoided, and we must refrain from a multitude of unnecessary matters no less than of words.

But just as the accuser, when he removes the fault from others, will use the topics of the defender, so the accused will use those topics which are given to the accuser, when he wishes to transfer the charge from himself to others. From the person, again, conjecture will be drawn if those matters which are assigned to persons are carefully considered, all of which we set forth in the first book. For from the name too some suspicion sometimes arises—and when we say "name," the surname too ought to be understood; for it concerns the certain and proper designation of a man—as if we should say that someone is called "Caldus" (Hot) for the reason that he is of rash and sudden counsel;

The narrative can be clear if, as each thing was first done, so it is first set forth, and the order of events and times is preserved, so that things are narrated as they were done, or as they might seem to have been done. Here we must consider that nothing be said confusedly, nothing intricately, that there be no passing off into another matter, no fetching from the very first, no extending to the end, and that nothing pertaining to the matter be passed over; and in general, the precepts which concern brevity are to be observed in this kind too. For often a matter is too little understood by the length rather than by the obscurity of the narrative. And clear words too must be used; about which kind of thing we must speak in the precepts on expression. The narrative will be plausible if those things appear in it which are wont to appear in reality; if the dignities of the persons are preserved; if the motives of the deeds are evident; if there seem to have been the means of doing them; if it is shown that the time was suitable, the space sufficient, the place opportune for the very matter about which the narration is made; if the matter is fitted both to the nature of those who act, and to the custom of ordinary men, and to the opinion of those who hear. And by these methods it can be made probable.
