For all these things—whether one is man or woman, of this or that state, of what ancestors, what blood-relations, what age, what mind, what body—which are assigned to nature, will pertain to making some conjecture. And from manner of life many suspicions are drawn, when it is inquired how and among whom and by whom one was brought up and educated, and with whom one lives, by what plan of life,

But besides this it will be necessary to consider that the narrative be not interposed either when it is harmful or when it does no good; or be not told out of place, or otherwise than the cause demands. It is harmful when the exposition of the very deed done meets with great offence, which it will be necessary to soften by arguing and pleading the cause. When this happens, it will be necessary to scatter the parts of the deed done, member by member, throughout the cause, and to fit each at once to its proper argument, so that the remedy may be at hand for the wound and the defence may at once mitigate the odium. The narrative does no good when, the matter having been set forth by our opponents, it is of no concern to us to narrate it again or in another way; or when those who are listening grasp the matter so well that it is of no concern to us to inform them otherwise. When this happens, the narrative must be entirely omitted. It is told out of place when it is not set in that part of the speech where the matter demands; about which kind of thing we shall treat when we speak of arrangement, for this belongs to arrangement. It is not told as the cause demands when either that which helps the opponent is set forth clearly and ornately, or that which helps our own side is stated obscurely and carelessly. Therefore, to avoid this fault, everything must be turned to the advantage of our own cause: passing over the contrary points which can be passed over, touching lightly upon those which must be stated, and narrating our own carefully and distinctly. And about the narrative enough seems to have been said; let us pass next to the partition.

by what domestic custom one lives. And from fortune an argument often arises, when it is considered whether one is slave or free, wealthy or poor, noble or ignoble, fortunate or unfortunate, a private person or in office, or has been, or will be; or, finally, when some one of those things is inquired into which are understood to be assigned to fortune. But since "condition" consists in some perfect and constant completeness of mind or body, in which kind are virtue, knowledge, and their contraries, the matter itself, once the case is set, will teach whether this topic too shows any suspicion. For the account of disposition is wont to carry with it a clear conjecture, such as love, anger, distress, for the reason that both their own force is understood and it is easy to recognize what consequence follows any of these.

A partition rightly made in a cause renders the whole speech clear and lucid. It has two parts, each of which greatly serves to open up the cause and to establish the controversy. One part is that which shows what is agreed upon with the opponents and what is left in controversy; from which something definite is set before the hearer, on which he ought to keep his mind fixed. The other is that in which a brief, distributed exposition is made of those matters of which we are going to speak; from which it comes about that the hearer holds in his mind certain definite matters, on the statement of which he understands that the speech will be concluded. Now it seems we must briefly say how each kind of partition should be used. The partition which shows what is agreed upon and what is not ought to incline that which is agreed upon to the advantage of one's own cause, in this manner: "That the mother was killed by her son is agreed between me and my opponents." Likewise on the contrary side: "That Agamemnon was killed by Clytemnestra is agreed." For here each man both stated what was agreed upon and yet looked to the advantage of his own cause. Then what is in controversy must be set down in the statement of the point for decision;

But a pursuit, since it is a constant occupation vehemently applied to some matter with great pleasure, easily yields that argument which the matter itself will require in the cause. Likewise from purpose some suspicion will be taken; for a purpose is a deliberate plan of doing or not doing something. Now deeds and accidents and speeches, which are all, as was said in the precepts of confirmation, distributed into three tenses, it will be easy to see whether they bring anything to confirm the conjecture of suspicion.

how this is to be found has been said before. The partition which contains a distributed exposition of the matters ought to have these qualities: brevity, completeness, and fewness. Brevity is when no word is taken up except the necessary one. This is useful in this kind for the reason that the hearer's mind is to be held by the matters themselves and the parts of the cause, not by words or extraneous ornaments. Completeness is that by which we embrace in the partition all the kinds of matter which fall within the cause and of which we must speak, so that no useful kind is left out, or introduced too late outside the partition—which is the most faulty and disgraceful thing. Fewness is preserved in the partition if the kinds of matters themselves are set down, and not confusedly involved with their parts. For a kind is that which embraces several parts, as "animal." A part is that which falls under a kind, as "horse." But often the same thing is a kind to one and a part to another. For "man" is a part of "animal," but a kind in relation to "Thebans" or "Trojans." This distinction is introduced rather carefully, so that, with the relation of kinds and parts made clear, fewness of kinds may be preserved in the partition. For he who makes a partition thus: "I shall show that through the desire, the audacity, and the avarice of our opponents all misfortunes have come upon the commonwealth," has failed to understand that, having set down a kind in the partition, he has mixed in a part of the kind. For desire is, doubtless, the kind of all the passions, and of this kind avarice is without doubt a part.

And these are the matters assigned to persons, all of which, gathered into one place, the accuser will have to use to discredit the man. For the cause of the deed has too little firmness, unless the mind of him who is accused is brought into such a suspicion that he may not seem to have shrunk from such a fault. For just as it avails nothing to discredit someone's mind, when no cause why he should sin intervened, so it is a slight thing that a cause of sin intervened, if the mind is shown to be akin to no less honourable a course. Therefore the accuser will have to discredit the life of him whom he accuses from his former deeds, and to show whether he has been convicted of any like fault before; if he cannot do this, whether he has come under any similar suspicion before, and most of all, if it can be done, whether, in a similar kind of matter, moved by some cause of the same sort, he has sinned, whether in an equally great matter, or in a greater, or in a lesser; as if someone, whom he says was induced by money to do the deed, can demonstrate some greedy act of his in some other matter.

This, then, must be avoided: that you should not set down in the same partition, as though it were some different and dissimilar part, that of which you have already set down the kind. But if several parts should fall under some kind, when it has been set down simply in the first partition of the cause, it will be distributed most conveniently at the time when we come to explain it in the pleading of the cause, after the partition. And this too pertains to fewness: that we should not say we are going to demonstrate more things than is enough, in this manner: "I shall show that our opponents both could do, and wished to do, and did do, what we charge"; for it is enough to show that they did it. Or that, when there is no partition in the cause, when something simple is in question, we should nevertheless use distribution—which can very rarely occur. And there are also other precepts of partitions which do not so greatly pertain to this oratorical use, which are found in philosophy, from which we have transferred these very ones that seemed appropriate—none of which we found in the other treatises. And it will be necessary to remember these precepts about partition throughout the whole speech, so that each part may be carried through in order, as it was set forth in the partition, and that, when all have been explained, the matter may be concluded, in such a way that nothing be brought in afterwards except the conclusion. In Terence the old man in the Andria makes a partition briefly and aptly of what he wishes the freedman to learn: "In this way you will learn both my son's life and my own plan, and what I wish you to do in this matter." And so, just as he proposed in the partition, so he narrates: first his son's life, "For after he had passed out of boyhood . . ."; then his own plan, "And now I am taking pains . . ."; then what he wishes Sosia to do, which he put last in the partition, he says last: "Now it is your task . . ." Therefore, just as here he approached each part first in turn and made an end of speaking when all were finished, so it pleases us both to approach the several parts and, when all are finished, to conclude. Now it seems we must give precepts on the confirmation next, as the order itself demands.

Likewise in every cause the accuser ought to join to that cause by which he says one was moved to sin the nature, or the manner of life, or the pursuit, or the fortune, or some one of those things which are assigned to persons; and from a different kind of faults too, if there shall be no opportunity of taking from a like kind, he ought to discredit the mind of the adversary: if you charge that he did it induced by avarice, and you cannot demonstrate that the one you accuse is avaricious, you may teach that he is akin to other vices, and that from this it is not to be wondered at that one who in that matter was base, or covetous, or wanton, has gone astray in this matter too. For as much as is taken away from the honour and authority of him who is accused, just so much is diminished from the resources of the whole defence.

The confirmation is that by which, by arguing, the speech adds credit, authority, and support to our cause. This part has definite precepts, which will be divided according to the several kinds of causes. Nevertheless it does not seem amiss first to set forth, in a mixed and confused way, a kind of forest and undifferentiated material of all the arguments, and afterwards to hand down how each kind of cause ought to be confirmed by the arguments drawn from it through all the methods of arguing. All matters are confirmed by argument either from that which is assigned to persons or from that which is assigned to actions. To persons we hold these things assigned: name, nature, manner of life, fortune, condition, disposition, pursuits, purposes, deeds, accidents, and speeches. The name is that which is given to each several person, by which each is called by his own proper and definite designation. Nature itself it is difficult to define;

If the accused cannot be demonstrated to be akin to any vice committed before, that topic will be introduced through which the judges must be exhorted to think the man's old reputation has nothing to do with the matter. For he concealed himself before, now he is manifestly caught; therefore this matter ought not to be judged by his former life, but his former life ought to be discredited by this matter; and either there was no power of sinning before, or no cause; or, if these things cannot be said, that last thing must be said—it is not surprising if he has now offended for the first time; for it must be that he who wishes to sin offends at some point for the first time. But if the life formerly led shall be unknown, with this topic passed over and the reason for passing it over demonstrated, the accusation must be confirmed at once with arguments.

but it is easier to enumerate those parts of it which we need for this treatment. These are partly in the divine, partly in the mortal class. Of the mortal, again, one part is reckoned in the human class, another in that of beasts. And the human class is considered both in respect of sex—whether male or female—and of nation, country, kinship, and age. As to nation: Greek or barbarian; country: Athenian or Spartan; kinship: from what ancestors, from what blood-relations; age: boy or youth, more advanced in years or old. Besides these, the advantages and disadvantages given by nature to mind or body are considered, in this manner: whether one is strong or weak, tall or short, handsome or deformed, swift or slow, keen or rather dull, of good memory or forgetful, courteous or uncouth, modest, patient, or the reverse; and in general, those things given by nature to mind and body will be considered. For the things acquired by effort pertain to the "condition," about which we must speak later. In manner of life one must consider with whom, by what custom, and under whose direction one has been brought up; what teachers of the liberal arts one has had, what instructors in living; what friends one keeps; in what occupation, gainful pursuit, or craft one is engaged; in what way one manages one's household; what one's domestic habits are. In fortune it is inquired whether one is slave or free, wealthy or poor, a private person or one in office: if in office, rightly or wrongfully; whether fortunate, famous, or the reverse; what children one has. And if the inquiry is about one no longer living, it will be necessary to consider also by what manner of death he was affected.

The defender, however, first, if he can, ought to demonstrate the life of him who is accused to be as honourable as possible. He will do this if he shall set forth some marked and ordinary services of his; of which kind are those toward parents, kinsmen, friends, connections, intimates; also those which are rarer and more exceptional, if he shall say that something was done by him with great labour or danger, or both, when there was no necessity, for duty's sake, either toward the commonwealth, or toward his parents, or toward some of those just set forth; finally, if he has offended in nothing, has withdrawn from no duty hindered by any desire. Which will be the more confirmed if, when it shall be said that there was the power of doing something less honourable with impunity, it shall be demonstrated that the will to do it was absent.

By "condition" we mean a constant and complete perfection of mind or body in some respect, such as the acquisition of virtue or of some art, or any knowledge, and likewise some advantage of body not given by nature but obtained by study and effort. Disposition is a momentary alteration of mind or body from some cause, such as joy, desire, fear, distress, sickness, weakness, and others found in the same class. A pursuit is an occupation of the mind, constant and vehemently applied to some object with great pleasure, such as that of philosophy, poetry, geometry, literature. A purpose is a deliberate plan of doing or not doing something. Deeds, accidents, and speeches are to be considered in respect of three tenses: what one did, what happened to one, what one said; or what one does, what happens to one, what one says; or what one will do, what will happen to one, what speech one will use. These, then, are the things which seem assigned to persons.

But this very kind will be the firmer if, in that very kind in which he is accused, he shall be demonstrated to have been blameless before: as if, when he is accused of having acted for avarice's sake, he be taught to have been least of all covetous of money in his whole life. Here that indignation will be introduced with great gravity, joined to an appeal to pity, through which it will be demonstrated to be a wretched and unworthy thing that, when the mind was in its whole life most remote from vices, one should think that that cause which is wont to drag bold men into wrong could have impelled even the most chaste man to sin; or that it is unfair and most ruinous to every best man that a life honourably led should not avail as much as possible at such a time, but that judgment should be made from a sudden charge, which can be fabricated however falsely, not from the life formerly led, which can neither be feigned to suit the moment nor in any way changed.

As to the things assigned to actions, some are connected with the action itself, some are considered in the conduct of the action, some are adjuncts of the action, and some follow the action. Connected with the action itself are those things which always seem fixed to the matter and cannot be separated from it. The first of these is a brief summary of the whole action, which contains the substance of the deed, in this manner: "the killing of a parent," "the betrayal of one's country"; then the motive of this summary, by which it is inquired why, and for what reason, and for the sake of what the deed was done; then the things which were done continuously before the deed, up to the action itself; then what was done in the very performance of the action; then what was done afterwards.

But if in the life formerly led there shall be some baseness, either it shall be said that he came falsely into that ill repute, from the envy or detraction or false opinion of some persons; or these things shall be attributed to imprudence, necessity, persuasion, youth, or some not malicious disposition of mind; or to a different kind of vices . . . , so that the mind may seem not wholly blameless, but remote from such a fault. But if in no way can the baseness or infamy of his life be softened by speech, it will be necessary to deny that the inquiry is about his life and morals, but about that charge on which he is accused; therefore, with his former deeds passed over, the matter which presses ought to be treated.

In the conduct of the action—which was the second topic of those assigned to actions—the following will be inquired into: place, time, manner, occasion, and means. The place in which the deed was done is considered with regard to the opportunity it seems to have offered for carrying out the action. And this opportunity is sought from the magnitude, the distance, the remoteness, the nearness, the solitude, the crowdedness, the nature of the place itself and of its neighbourhood and of the whole region; and also from these attributions: whether the place is or was sacred or profane, public or private, another's or belonging to the very person concerned.

From the deed itself, again, suspicions will be drawn if the conduct of the whole affair is tried out in all its parts; and these suspicions will proceed partly from the affair separately, partly in common from the persons and the affair. They can be drawn from the affair if we carefully consider those matters which are assigned to affairs. From these, then, all the kinds of them seem to suit this issue, and most of the parts of the kinds.

Time—that is, what we now mean by it; for to define it in a general sense is difficult—is a certain portion of eternity, with some definite designation of a yearly, monthly, daily, or nightly space. In this both past times are considered: both those things which, either through age, have become obsolete or seem incredible, so that they are now reckoned among fables; and those things which, though done long ago and removed from our memory, nevertheless produce belief that they have been truly handed down, because there are sure records of them in writing; and those things which have been done recently, which most people can know; and likewise those which are at hand at present and are happening at this very moment; and those which follow, in which it can be considered what will be sooner and what later. And likewise, in observing time generally, its length must be considered. For often it is necessary to measure the action against the time, and to see whether either the magnitude of the action or the multitude of matters could be carried through in that time.

First, then, it will be necessary to see what things are connected with the affair itself, that is, what cannot be separated from the matter. On this topic it will be enough to have carefully considered what was done before the matter, from which the hope of accomplishing seems to have arisen and the means of doing it to have been sought; what was done in the very performance of the matter; what followed afterwards. Then the conduct of the affair itself must be handled thoroughly. For this kind of those matters which are assigned to the affair was set forth by us in the second place.

The occasion is a portion of time having in itself a suitable opportunity for doing or not doing something. Therefore it differs from time in this: for in kind both are understood to be the same, but in "time" a space is in some manner indicated, which is observed in years, or in a year, or in some part of a year, while in "occasion" a certain opportunity for doing something, joined to a space of time, is understood. Therefore, though it is the same in kind, it becomes something else, which differs, as we said, in a certain part and aspect. It is divided into three kinds: the public, the common, and the individual. The public is that which the whole community for some reason frequents, such as games, a festal day, war. The common is that which befalls all at about the same time, such as harvest, vintage, heat, cold. The individual is that which for some reason is wont to befall someone privately, such as marriage, sacrifice, a funeral, a banquet, sleep.

In this kind, therefore, will be observed place, time, occasion, means; the force of each one of which was carefully explained in the precepts of confirmation. Therefore, lest we either seem not to have given warning here, or to have said the same things again, we shall briefly suggest what ought to be considered in each part. In place, then, the opportunity; in time, the length; in occasion, the convenience suitable for doing; in means, the abundance and the power of those things on account of which something is done more easily, or without which it cannot be accomplished at all—these must be considered.

The manner is that in which it is inquired in what way and with what intent the deed was done. Its parts are prudence and imprudence. The account of prudence is sought from those things which one did secretly, openly, by force, or by persuasion. Imprudence, however, is referred to purgation, whose parts are ignorance, accident, and necessity, and to a disposition of mind, that is, to distress, anger, love, and the rest which are found in a like class. Means are those things by which something is more easily done, or without which something cannot be accomplished. By an "adjunct of the action" is understood that which is greater, and that which is less, and that which is equally great, and that which is similar to the action under discussion, and that which is contrary, and that which is disparate, and the kind, the part, and the result. The greater, the less, and the equally great are considered from the force, the number, and the form of the action, just as from the stature of the body.

Then it must be seen what is an adjunct of the affair, that is, what is greater, what less, what equally great, what similar; from which a certain conjecture is drawn, if it shall be carefully considered in what way greater, lesser, equally great, and similar matters are wont to be done. In this kind the result too must be seen, that is, what is wont to come of each thing must be greatly considered, such as fear, joy, faltering, audacity.

The similar is judged from a comparable appearance, or from a nature that can be compared and likened. The contrary is that which, set in a different kind, is most distant from the same thing to which it is called contrary, as cold to heat, death to life. The disparate is that which is separated from some matter by the prefix of a negation, in this manner: "to be wise" and "not to be wise." The kind is that which embraces some parts, as "desire." The part is that which falls under a kind, as "love," "avarice." The result is the outcome of some action, in which it is wont to be inquired what has come, comes, or will come of each thing. Therefore in this class, in order that it may be conveniently gathered in the mind beforehand what will come about, it must be considered what is wont to come of each thing, in this manner: from arrogance, hatred; from insolence, arrogance.

The fourth part of those matters which we said were assigned to affairs was the consequence. In it are inquired those things which follow the deed done, at once or after an interval. In this we shall see whether there is any custom, any law, any agreement, any art or use or practice of the matter, any approval or disapproval of men; from which sometimes some suspicion is elicited. But there are other suspicions which are taken in common from the attributes both of affairs and of persons. For both from fortune and from nature and from manner of life, pursuit, deeds, accident, speeches, purpose, and from the condition of mind or body, most things pertain to those same matters which can make a thing credible or incredible,

The fourth part of those things which we said were assigned to actions is the consequence. In this are inquired those things which follow the action performed: first, what name it is fitting to give to what was done; then who are the originators and inventors of that deed, and who, finally, are the approvers and rivals of its authority and invention; then whether there is any law, custom, agreement, judgment, science, or art concerning that matter or that kind of matter; then its nature—whether it commonly happens, or rarely and exceptionally; afterwards, whether men have been wont by their authority to approve such deeds or to take offence at them; and the other things which are wont to follow some deed in like manner, either at once or after an interval. Then, finally, attention must be paid to whether any of those things follow which are placed among the elements of honour or of advantage; about which we must speak more distinctly in the deliberative kind of cause. And these, in general, are the matters we have mentioned as assigned to actions.

and are joined with the suspicion of the deed. For most of all it is fitting to inquire, in this issue, first whether anything could have been done; then whether it could have been done by anyone else; then the means, of which we spoke before; then whether it is the kind of deed which one would necessarily have repented, which had no hope of concealment; then the necessity, in which it is inquired whether it was necessary either for it to be done, or to be done thus. Part of these pertain to purpose, which is assigned to persons, as in that case which we set forth: before the matter—that he attached himself so companionably on the journey, that he sought an occasion for conversation, that he turned aside together, and then dined. In the matter—night, sleep. After the matter—that he went out alone, that he left so companionable a man so calmly, that he had a bloody sword.

Now every argument which is drawn from those topics which we have mentioned ought to be either probable or necessary. For—to describe it briefly—an argument seems to be something discovered from some class, showing some matter either probably or demonstrating it necessarily. Those things are demonstrated necessarily which cannot be or be proved otherwise than is stated, in this manner: "If she has given birth, she has lain with a man." This kind of arguing, which deals with necessary demonstration, is handled in speaking chiefly by the dilemma, or by enumeration, or by simple inference.

Again, whether a method of doing seems to have been carefully held and devised, or so rashly that it is not probable that anyone went forward to a crime so rashly. In which it is inquired whether it could have been done more conveniently in some other way, or managed by chance. For often, if money, aids, helpers are lacking, the means of doing does not seem to have existed. In this way, if we attend carefully, we understand that these things which are assigned to affairs, and those which are assigned to persons, are fitted to one another. Here it is neither easy nor necessary, as in the earlier parts, to distinguish in what way each ought to handle the matter as accuser and in what way as defender. It is not necessary, for the reason that, the case being set, the matter itself will teach what suits each, for those who will not think they are going to find everything here,

The dilemma is that in which, whichever you grant, you are confuted, in this manner: "If he is wicked, why do you employ him? If he is good, why do you accuse him?" Enumeration is that in which, several things being set forth and the rest invalidated, the one remaining is necessarily established, in this manner: "He must have been killed by this man either for the sake of enmity, or fear, or hope, or the favour of some friend; or, if none of these is the case, he was not killed by this man; for a crime cannot be undertaken without a motive: if there was neither enmity nor any fear nor hope of any advantage, and the death of that man did not concern any friend of this one—it remains, then, that he was not killed by this man." Simple inference is composed of a necessary consequence, in this manner: "If you say that I did that thing at that time, and yet at that very time I was beyond the sea, it remains that I not only did not do what you say, but could not even have done it." And it will be necessary to see carefully that this kind cannot in any way be refuted, so that the confirmation may not merely have the form of an argument and a certain likeness of necessary inference, but the argument itself may rest on a necessary principle.

Therefore it will be fitting to consider these things which we have set forth. But the mind will more easily light upon invention if it shall handle often and carefully both its own narrative and the adversary's of the deed done, and, eliciting whatever suspicion each part holds, shall consider with what purpose, with what hope of accomplishing, each thing was done; why in this way rather than that; why by this man rather than that; why with no helper, or why with this one; why no one was privy, or why someone was, or why this one; why this was done before; why this in the affair itself, why this after the affair; whether it was done deliberately, or followed the matter itself; whether the speech is consistent either with the matter or with itself; whether this is a sign of this matter or of that, or of both, and rather of which; what was done which ought not to have been, or not done which ought to have been.

The probable is that which generally is wont to happen, or which rests on opinion, or which has in itself some likeness to these, whether it be false or true. In the class of what generally is wont to happen, the probable is of this kind: "If she is a mother, she loves her child; if he is greedy, he disregards an oath." In that which rests on opinion, the probabilities are of this kind: "Punishments are prepared for the impious in the lower world; those who devote themselves to philosophy do not believe that there are gods." Likeness is observed chiefly in contraries, in parallels, and in those matters which fall under the same principle. In contraries, in this manner: "For if it is fitting that those who have done harm unintentionally should be pardoned, those who have done good of necessity ought not to be thanked." When the mind shall consider all the parts of the whole affair with this attention, then those very topics gathered into one place will come forward, of which we have spoken before; and then, now from single, now from joined topics, sure arguments will arise, part of which arguments will turn on the probable, part on the necessary kind. But often there are added to conjecture interrogations, testimonies, rumours, all of which each side will have to twist to the advantage of his own cause by a similar method of precepts. For both from interrogation and from testimony and from some rumour, suspicions ought to be drawn by a like method, as from the cause, from the person, and from the deed.

"For as a place without a harbour cannot be safe for ships, so a mind without good faith cannot be steadfast for friends." In those matters which fall under the same principle, the probable is considered in this manner: "For if it is not disgraceful for the Rhodians to lease out the harbour-tax, neither is it disgraceful for Hermocreon to contract for it." These things are sometimes true, in this way: "Since there is a scar, there was a wound"; sometimes probable, in this manner: "If there was much dust on his shoes, he must have been coming from a journey." Now everything probable that is taken for an argument is—to distribute it into certain parts—either a sign, or a credible thing, or a precedent (judgment), or a comparable thing.

Therefore those too seem to us to err who think this kind of suspicion needs no art, and those who think instruction ought to be given about this kind otherwise than about all conjecture. For every conjecture must be taken from the same topics. For both the motive and the truth of him who said something in interrogation, and of him who said something in testimony, and of rumour itself, will be found from the same attributes. But in every cause part of the arguments is attached only to that cause which is being pleaded, and so drawn from it that it cannot conveniently enough be transferred separately from it into all causes of the same kind; but part is more widely ranging and adapted either to all causes of the same kind or to most.

A sign is that which falls under some sense and indicates something which seems to have proceeded from it, which either preceded, or occurred in the action itself, or followed afterwards, and yet needs testimony and weightier confirmation, such as blood, flight, pallor, dust, and the like. The credible is that which, without any witness, is established by the opinion of the hearer, in this manner: "There is no one who does not desire his children to be safe and happy." The precedent is a matter approved by the assent, or the authority, or the judgment of someone or of several. It is observed in three kinds: the religious, the common, and the approved. The religious is that which men under oath have judged according to the laws. The common is that which all men have commonly approved and followed, of this kind: that one should rise before one's elders, that one should pity suppliants. The approved is that which men, when it was doubtful how it ought to be regarded, have settled by their own authority: as the deed of the elder Gracchus, which the Roman people, who made him consul after his censorship, although as censor he had done something without the knowledge of his colleague, thereby approved.

These arguments, then, which can be transferred to many causes, we name commonplaces. For a commonplace contains either some amplification of a certain matter—as if someone should wish to show that he who has killed a parent is worthy of the greatest punishment; which topic must not be used unless the cause has been pleaded out—or of a doubtful matter, which from the contrary side too has probable methods of arguing, as that one ought to believe suspicions, and, on the contrary, that one ought not to believe suspicions. And part of the commonplaces is introduced through indignation or through appeal to pity, of which we have spoken before, part through some probable method on either side.

The comparable is that which contains, in different matters, some similar principle. Its parts are three: the figure (analogy), the comparison, and the example. The figure is a passage demonstrating a likeness of bodies or natures. The comparison is a passage comparing one matter with another by likeness. The example is that which confirms or invalidates a matter by the authority or fortune of some man or affair. Examples and descriptions of these will be made known in the precepts on expression. And the source of confirmation, as opportunity allowed, has now been laid open, and demonstrated no less clearly than the nature of the matter permitted. But how each issue, and each part of an issue, and every controversy, whether it rests on reasoning or on writing, ought to be handled, and what arguments suit each, we shall state one by one in the second book, concerning each several kind. For the present we have only scattered, in a confused and mixed way, the elements, modes, and parts of arguing; afterwards we shall, in a distinct and selective manner, arrange from this abundance what suits each kind of cause.

But the speech is distinguished and illuminated most of all by introducing commonplaces rarely, and at some point already confirmed by those surer arguments. For then it is permitted to say something in common, when some topic proper to the cause has been carefully handled, and the mind of the hearer is either renewed for what remains, or, all having now been said, is roused. But all the ornaments of expression, in which both sweetness and gravity chiefly consist, and all those things which in the invention of matters and thoughts have some dignity, are conferred upon commonplaces.

And while every argument can be discovered from these topics, to adorn what has been discovered and to mark it off into definite parts is both most delightful and supremely necessary, and most neglected by the writers on the art. Therefore it seemed right that I too should speak of this instruction in this place, so that to invention the method of arguing might be joined. And this whole topic must be considered with great care and diligence, because the matter is not only of great usefulness, but the difficulty of teaching it is also very great.

Therefore, just as causes have their commonplaces, so do many orators too. For they cannot be handled ornately and weightily, as their nature requires, except by those who, by much practice, have prepared for themselves a great abundance of words and thoughts. And let this be said by us in common about every kind of commonplace; now we shall set forth what commonplaces are wont to fall upon the conjectural issue: that one ought to believe suspicions and ought not; that one ought to believe rumours and ought not; that one ought to believe witnesses and ought not; that one ought to believe interrogations and ought not; that the life formerly led ought to be regarded and ought not; that it belongs to the same man who sinned in that matter to have committed this too, and that it does not belong to the same; that the cause ought most of all to be regarded and ought not. And these, and any commonplaces of this kind which arise from a proper argument,

Every argument, then, must be handled either by induction or by reasoning (deduction). Induction is a discourse which, by means of matters not in doubt, wins the assent of the person with whom it is carried on; by which assent it brings it about that some doubtful matter is approved by him on account of its likeness to those matters to which he has assented. For example, in Aeschines the Socratic, Socrates shows that Aspasia conversed with the wife of Xenophon and with Xenophon himself: "Tell me, I pray, wife of Xenophon, if your neighbour had better gold than you have, would you prefer hers or your own?" "Hers," she said. "What, if she had clothing and the rest of a woman's adornment of greater value than you have, would you prefer your own or hers?" She answered, "Hers, of course." "Come then," she said, "what if she had a better husband than you have, would you prefer your own husband or hers?" Here the woman blushed.

are divided into opposite sides. But there is a definite topic of the accuser, through which he magnifies the atrocity of the deed, and another, through which he denies that one ought to pity the wicked; of the defender, through which the calumny of the accusers is shown with indignation, and through which pity is captured with appeal. These, and all the other commonplaces, are taken from the same precepts as the other arguments; but those are handled more finely, more subtly, and more keenly, while these are handled more weightily and more ornately, with both excellent words and excellent thoughts. For in those the end is that what is said may seem true; in these, although this too ought to appear, nevertheless the end is grandeur. Now let us pass to another issue.

But Aspasia began a conversation with Xenophon himself. "I pray, Xenophon," she said, "if your neighbour had a better horse than yours is, would you prefer your own horse or his?" "His," he said. "What, if he had a better farm than you have, which farm would you, after all, prefer to have?" "The better one, of course," he said. "What, if he had a better wife than you have, would you prefer your own or his?" And here Xenophon too himself fell silent. Then Aspasia said: "Since each of you has failed to answer me that one thing alone which I alone wished to hear, I myself will say what each of you is thinking. For you, woman, wish to have the best husband, and you, Xenophon, most of all wish to have the choicest wife. Therefore, unless you bring it about that there be no better man and no choicer woman on earth, you will surely always most greatly long for that which you think best." Here, since assent was given to matters not in doubt, it came about, on account of the likeness, that even that which would seem doubtful, if anyone inquired into it separately, was granted as certain on account of the method of questioning.

When there is a controversy of name, because the meaning of the term must be defined in words, the issue is called definitional. Let this case be set before us as an example of this kind: Gaius Flaminius—he who as consul mismanaged affairs in the Second Punic War—when he was tribune of the people, against the will of the senate and altogether contrary to the wishes of all the aristocrats, was bringing an agrarian law before the people through sedition. His own father led him down from the platform while he was holding an assembly of the people; he is arraigned for treason. The charge is: "You diminished the majesty of the state, because you led down a tribune of the people from the platform." The rebuttal is: "I did not diminish the majesty." The question is: "Did he diminish the majesty?" The reason: "For I used that power over my son which I had." The invalidation of the reason: "But he who weakens the tribunician power—that is, the power of the people—by paternal power—that is, a kind of private power—diminishes the majesty." The point for decision is: "Does he diminish the majesty who uses paternal power against the tribunician power?" To this point for decision all the arguments will have to be brought.

Socrates used this manner of discourse very much, for the reason that he himself wished to bring forward nothing to persuade, but preferred to draw some conclusion from what his interlocutor had granted him, which the other had necessarily to approve from what he had already conceded. In this kind it seems we must first lay down this precept: that what we introduce by way of likeness should be such that it must be granted. For from that which we shall ask to have granted to us must not be doubtful as our doubtful point. Next, that which the induction is made to confirm must, we must see, be like those matters which we have introduced before as though not doubtful; for it will profit us nothing to have had something granted us before, if it is unlike that for the sake of which we wished it granted first. Then we must see that the hearer does not perceive whither those first inductions tend and at what conclusion they are going to arrive.

And lest anyone perhaps suppose that we do not understand that another issue too falls upon this case, we take only that part on which precepts must be given by us. But with all the parts explained in this book, anyone, in every cause, if he shall attend carefully, will see all the issues and their parts and the controversies, if any perhaps fall upon them; for we shall prescribe about all. The first topic of the accuser, then, is a brief and clear definition, drawn from the opinion of men, of that name about whose meaning the inquiry is, in this manner: "To diminish the majesty is to detract something from the dignity, or grandeur, or power of the people, or of those to whom the people has given power." This, so briefly set forth, must be confirmed with more words and reasons, and it must be shown that it is as you have described. Afterwards it will be necessary to join to what you have defined the deed of him who is accused, and from what you have shown to be, for instance, "to diminish the majesty," to teach that the adversary has diminished the majesty, and to confirm this whole topic with a commonplace, through which the atrocity or unworthiness of the very deed, or its guilt altogether, is magnified with indignation.

For the man who sees that, if he rightly assents to the matter about which he is first asked, he must necessarily grant that other matter too which displeases him, generally, either by not answering or by answering badly, does not allow the questioning to proceed further. Therefore by the method of questioning he must be led, unawares, from what he has granted to what he does not wish to grant. But the conclusion must either be passed over in silence, or be granted, or be denied. If it is denied, either the likeness of those matters which were granted before must be shown, or another induction must be used. If it is granted, the argument must be concluded. If it is met with silence, an answer must be elicited; or, since silence imitates confession, the argument must be concluded just as if it had been granted. So this kind of arguing becomes threefold: the first part consists of one or more likenesses; the second of that which we wish granted, for the sake of which the likenesses were employed; the third of the conclusion, which either confirms the concession or shows what is inferred from it.

Afterwards the adversaries' description must be weakened. And it will be weakened if it is demonstrated to be false. This will be taken from the opinion of men, when it is considered in what way and in what matters men are wont, in the custom of writing or speaking, to use that word. Likewise it will be weakened if it is shown that the approval of that description is base or useless, and what disadvantages will follow if it is granted—this, again, will be taken from the elements of honour and of usefulness, of which we shall speak in the precepts of deliberation—and if we compare the adversaries' definition with our own, and demonstrate ours to be true, honourable, useful, theirs the contrary.

But because to some it will not seem to have been demonstrated clearly enough unless we add some example from the civil kind of cause, it seems we should use an example of this kind too—not because the precept differs, or this is to be used otherwise in conversation than in pleading, but to satisfy the wishes of those who cannot recognize in one place what they have seen in another, unless it is pointed out. Therefore in this cause, which is well known among the Greeks—when Epaminondas, the general of the Thebans, since he did not hand over the army to the man who had succeeded him by law as commander, and, having kept the army for a few days contrary to the law, utterly defeated the Spartans—the accuser will be able to use argument by induction, when he defends the letter of the law against its intent, in this manner:

But we shall seek similar matters, in a greater or lesser or equal affair, from which our description may be affirmed. Now if several matters shall have to be defined—as if it be inquired whether one is a thief or a temple-robber who has stolen sacred vessels from a private place—several definitions must be used; then the cause must be handled by a like method. But the commonplace is against the wickedness of him who has tried to arrogate to himself the power not only over things but even over words, and both does what he wishes and calls what he has done by whatever name he wishes. Then the first topic of the defender is likewise a brief and clear description of the name, drawn from the opinion of men, in this manner: "To diminish the majesty is to administer something of public affairs when you do not have the power." Then a confirmation of this; afterwards a separation of his own deed from that definition.

"If, judges, what Epaminondas says the framer of the law intended were to be written into the law, and this exception added—'except in case someone should fail to hand over the army for the sake of the commonwealth'—would you permit it? I think not. What, if you yourselves were to order this same exception to be written into the law, for the sake of his honour, without the people's command—a thing most remote from your scruple and your wisdom—would the Theban people permit it to be done? Surely it would not permit it. Then, what it is impious to write into the law, would it seem right to you to follow as though it were written? I know your understanding; it cannot seem so, judges. But if the framer's intent cannot be corrected in writing either by him or by you, see whether it be not far more unworthy that what cannot even be changed by a word should be changed in fact and by your judgment." And about induction enough seems to have been said for the present.

Then the commonplace through which the usefulness or honour of the deed is increased. Then follows the refutation of the adversaries' definition, which is accomplished from all those same topics which we prescribed to the accuser; and the rest will afterwards be introduced in the same way, except the commonplace. But the defender's commonplace will be that through which he expresses indignation that the accuser, for the sake of his own peril, tries not only to alter things but even to change words. For those commonplaces indeed which are taken for the sake of demonstrating the calumny of the accusers, or of capturing pity, or of expressing indignation at a deed, or of deterring from pity, are drawn from the magnitude of the peril, not from the kind of cause. Therefore they fall not upon every cause, but upon every kind of cause. We made mention of them in the conjectural issue, and we shall use them by introduction when the cause shall require.

Now let us next consider the force and nature of reasoning. Reasoning is a discourse which draws something probable from the matter itself, which, when set forth and recognized in itself, confirms itself by its own force and reason. Those who have thought this kind ought to be considered more carefully, while following the same practice in speaking, have disagreed somewhat in their method of teaching. For some have said it has five parts, others have thought it could be divided into no more than three parts. It seems not amiss to set forth their controversy along with the reasoning of each side. For it is brief, and not of such a kind that either side is thought to say nothing at all, and this topic seems to us by no means to be neglected in speaking.

But when the action seems to need transfer or change, because either he who ought is not bringing it, or not against the man against whom he ought, or not before those before whom, or under the law under which, with the penalty with which, on the charge on which, at the time at which he ought, the issue is called translative. We should need very many examples of it if we were to seek out the several kinds of transfers; but because the method of the precepts is similar, we must dispense with a multitude of examples. And in our own practice it happens, for many reasons, that transfers fall out rather rarely. For many actions are excluded by the praetor's exceptions, and we have the civil law so established that he loses his case who has not brought it in the way he ought.

Those who think it ought to be divided into five parts say that first it is fitting to set forth the substance of the argument, in this manner: "Those things which are managed by design are managed better than those which are conducted without design." This they count the first part; and they hold that it ought next to be confirmed by various reasons and in the most copious words possible, in this manner: "That household which is governed by design is furnished and equipped with all things better than that which is managed rashly and without any design. An army over which a wise and skilful general is set is in all respects more conveniently governed than one which is managed by the folly and rashness of someone. The same is the case with a ship. For that ship completes its course best which has the most skilful helmsman."

Therefore they are mostly engaged in at law. For there both exceptions are demanded, and the power of bringing an action is given, and the whole framing of private suits is established. But in the trials themselves they fall out more rarely; and yet, if at any time they do fall out, they are of such a kind that of themselves they have less firmness, but are confirmed by taking up some other issue: as in a certain trial, when the name of a certain poisoning had been laid, and, because the charge of parricide had been entered, the case had been received out of the ordinary course, but in the accusation certain other charges were confirmed by witnesses and arguments, while mention of parricide alone had been made, the defender ought to dwell much and long on this very point: that, since nothing had been demonstrated about the slaying of a parent, it was an unworthy thing to afflict the accused with that penalty with which parricides are afflicted; but that this, if he were condemned, must necessarily be done, since both this had been entered in the case and on that account the name had been received out of the ordinary course.

When the proposition has been confirmed in this way, and two parts of the reasoning have passed, in the third part they say one must assume, from the force of the proposition, that which one wishes to show, in this manner: "But nothing of all things is managed better than the whole universe." To this assumption, in the fourth place, they further add another confirmation, in this manner: "For the risings and settings of the constellations preserve a certain fixed order, and the yearly changes not only always come about in the same way from a kind of necessity, but are also adapted to the advantages of all things; and the alternations of day and night, never changed in any respect, have never done any harm: all of which are signs that the nature of the universe is governed by no ordinary design." In the fifth place they introduce the conclusion, which either infers only that which is gathered from all the parts, in this manner: "By design, therefore, the universe is governed"; or, having drawn the proposition and assumption together briefly into one place, adds what is inferred from these, in this manner: "But if those things are managed better which are managed by design than those which are managed without design, and nothing of all things is managed better than the whole universe, then by design the universe is governed." So they hold the argument to be of five parts.

If, therefore, the accused ought not to be afflicted with that penalty, neither ought he to be condemned, since that penalty necessarily follows condemnation. Here the defender, by introducing a change of penalty from the translative kind, will weaken the whole accusation. Nevertheless, in defending the other charges too, he will confirm the transfer by the conjectural issue. But let an example of transfer set in a case be of this kind: when certain men had come armed to do violence, certain others stood ready against them armed, and one of the armed men cut off with his sword the hand of a certain Roman knight who was resisting. He whose hand was cut off brings an action for assault. He against whom the action is brought demands from the praetor an exception: "except in so far as a prejudgment may be made against the defendant in a capital matter."

But those who think it of three parts do not think the argument ought to be handled otherwise, but they find fault with the division of these others. For they deny that the confirmations of the proposition and of the assumption ought to be separated from them, and they hold that neither the proposition is complete nor the assumption perfect, in their view, which is not confirmed by a proof. Therefore what those others count as two parts, the proposition and the proof, seems to them one part, the proposition; which, if it is not proved, is not the proposition of an argument. Likewise what is called by those others the assumption and the proof of the assumption, the same seems to them the assumption alone. So it comes about that the same argument, handled in the same way, seems to some of three parts, to others of five parts. Hence it happens that the matter pertains not so much to the practice of speaking as to the theory of teaching.

Here he who brings the action demands a plain trial; the other, against whom the action is brought, says an exception ought to be added. The question is: "Is the exception to be made or not?" The reason: "For a prejudgment ought not to be made, in a suit for recovery, of that crime about which inquiry is held among the assassins." The invalidation of the reason: "Such are the assaults that it is unworthy not to be judged on them at the very first opportunity." The point for decision: "Is the atrocity of the assaults a sufficient cause why, while it is being judged, a prejudgment should be made about some greater crime for which a trial has been arranged?" And this indeed is the example. But in every cause it will be necessary for each side to inquire by whom, and through whom, and in what way, and at what time it is fitting either to bring or to judge the action, or to settle anything about that matter.

To us, however, that division seems more convenient which is distributed into five parts, which all those derived from Aristotle and Theophrastus have chiefly followed. For just as that former kind of arguing, which is taken by way of induction, was handled chiefly by Socrates and the Socratics, so this, which is polished by reasoning, was practised most by Aristotle and Theophrastus, and then by those rhetoricians who have been thought the most elegant and most artful. But why we approve that division more, it seems we must say, lest we be thought to have followed it rashly; and we must say it briefly, lest in matters of this kind we linger longer than the principle of teaching demands.

This will have to be taken from the parts of law, about which we must speak later, and one must reason what is wont to be done in similar matters, and see whether out of malice one thing is being done and another pretended, or out of folly, or out of necessity, because one cannot proceed otherwise, or whether by an opportunity for proceeding the trial or the action has been so framed, or whether the matter is rightly conducted without any such thing. But the commonplace against him who introduces a transfer is: that he flees the trial and the penalty because he distrusts his case. And from the transfer itself: that there will be confusion of everything if matters are not conducted and brought to trial in the way they ought; that is, if either an action is brought against one against whom it ought not, or with another penalty, on another charge, at another time; and that this principle pertains to the confusion of all trials. These three issues, then, which have no parts, will be handled in this manner. Now let us consider the general issue and its parts.

If in a certain argument it is enough to use the proposition and there is no need to add a proof of the proposition, but in another argument the proposition is weak unless a proof is added, then the proof is something separate from the proposition. For that which can be both joined to and separated from something cannot be the same as that to which it is joined and from which it is separated. But there is a certain argument in which the proposition does not need a proof, and another in which it avails nothing without a proof, as we shall show. The proof, then, is separate from the proposition. And what we have promised will be shown in this manner: a proposition which contains in itself something evident, which must necessarily stand fast among all men, it is of no use to wish to prove and confirm. Such a one is of this kind:

When, both the deed and the name of the deed being granted, and no controversy of action being raised, the force and nature and kind of the affair itself is inquired into, we call it the general issue. We have said that its first parts seem to us to be two, the negotial and the juridical. The negotial is that which has, in the affair itself, an implicit controversy of the civil law. It is of this kind: a certain man made a ward his heir; but the ward died before he came into the management of his own affairs. About the inheritance which came to the ward there is a controversy between those who are the secondary heirs of the ward's father and the kinsmen of the ward. The possession is the secondary heirs'. The charge of the kinsmen is: "It is our money, about which he, whose kinsmen we are, did not make a will." The rebuttal is: "Nay, it is ours, who are heirs by the father's will." The question is: "To which side does it belong?" The reason: "For the father wrote a will both for himself and for his son, while the latter was a ward. Therefore the things which were the son's must, by the father's will, become ours." The invalidation of the reason: "Nay, the father wrote for himself, and ordered the secondary heir to be his own heir, not his son's. Therefore, apart from what was his own, it cannot, by his will, be yours." The point for decision: "Can anyone make a will about a ward son's property? Or are the secondary heirs the heirs of the head of the household himself, and not also of his ward son?"

"If, on the day on which that murder was committed at Rome, I was at Athens on that day, I could not have been present at the murder." Because this is evidently true, it is of no use to prove it. Therefore the assumption ought at once to be made, in this manner: "But I was at Athens on that day." If this is not established, it needs proof; and when this has been brought in, the conclusion follows. There is, then, a certain proposition which does not need proof. For what is the use of showing that there is a certain one which does need it, since this is easily evident to anyone? But if this is so, from this and from what we had proposed it is inferred that the proof is something separate from the proposition. But if this is so, it is false that the argument is no more than threefold.

And it is not amiss to give warning here of this, which pertains to many things, lest it be said either nowhere or everywhere. There are causes which have several reasons in a simple issue; which happens when that which was done, or which is defended, can seem right or probable for several reasons, as in this very case. For let this reason be assumed by the heirs: "For there cannot be several heirs of one piece of property for dissimilar reasons, nor has it ever happened that of the same property one was heir by will, another by law."

In a like manner it is clear that the other proof too is separate from the assumption. If in a certain argument it is enough to use the assumption and there is no need to add a proof to the assumption, but in another argument the assumption is weak unless a proof is added, then the proof is something separate, outside the assumption. But there is a certain argument in which the assumption does not need a proof, and another in which it avails nothing without a proof, as we shall show. The proof, then, is separate from the assumption.

The invalidation will be this: "It is not one piece of property, for the reason that the one was already the ward's, acquired anew, of which no one was written heir in that will, in case anything should befall the ward; and about the other the will of the father, even now dead, was of the greatest force, which, the ward now being dead, granted it to his own heirs." The point for decision is: "Was it one piece of property?" Or, if they shall have used this invalidation—that there can be several heirs of one piece of property for dissimilar reasons, and that the controversy is about that very thing—the point for decision arises: "Can there be several heirs of the same property by dissimilar kinds?" Therefore in one issue it has been understood how both reasons and invalidations of reasons, and on that account several points for decision, arise.

And we shall show what we have promised, in this manner: an assumption which contains a truth evident to all needs no proof. Such a one is of this kind: "If one ought to wish to be wise, it is fitting to apply oneself to philosophy." Here the proposition needs proof; for it is not evident, nor does it stand fast among all men, because many think that philosophy is of no benefit, and very many even that it is harmful. The assumption is evident; for it is this: "But one ought to wish to be wise." Because this is perceived of itself and is understood to be true, it is of no use to prove it. Therefore the argument must at once be concluded. There is, then, a certain assumption which does not need proof; for that a certain one does need it is evident. The proof, then, is separate from the assumption. It is false, therefore, that the argument is no more than threefold.

Now let us see the precepts of this kind. Both sides, or even all sides, if more than two contend, must consider from what things law is composed. Its beginning, then, seems to be drawn from nature; then some things came into custom from a consideration of usefulness, either clear to us or obscure; afterwards some things, approved by custom or indeed seen to be useful, were sanctioned by laws. And that is the law of nature which not opinion, but a certain innate force, brings to us, such as religion, dutiful affection, gratitude, requital, observance, truth.

And from these things this is now evident: that there is a certain argument in which neither the proposition nor the assumption needs proof—of this kind, to set down something definite and brief by way of example: "If wisdom is to be sought above all, folly is to be avoided above all; but wisdom is to be sought above all; therefore folly is to be avoided above all." Here both the proposition and the assumption are evident; therefore neither needs proof. From all these things this is evident: that the proof is sometimes added and sometimes not added. From which it is recognized that the proof is contained neither in the proposition nor in the assumption, but that each, set in its proper place, holds its own force as something fixed and proper to it. But if this is so, they have divided rightly who have distributed the argument into five parts.

They call "religion" that which is in fear and ceremony of the gods; "dutiful affection," that which counsels us to preserve a kindly duty toward our country, or our parents, or others joined by blood; "gratitude," that which holds the observance of memory and requital of services, and of honour, and of friendships; "requital," through which by defending or avenging we drive off violence and insult from ourselves and from ours who ought to be dear to us, and through which we punish offences; "observance," through which we revere and honour those who excel in age, or wisdom, or honour, or some dignity; "truth," through which we take care that nothing be, or have been, or be about to be otherwise than we have affirmed.

There are, then, five parts of that argument which is handled by reasoning: the proposition, by which that topic is briefly set forth from which all the force of the reasoning ought to flow; the proof, by which what has been briefly set forth, confirmed by reasons, is made more probable and clearer; the assumption, by which that which, drawn from the proposition, serves to demonstrate the point, is assumed; the proof of the assumption, by which what has been assumed is confirmed by reasons; the conclusion, by which what is gathered from the whole argument is briefly set forth. The argument which has the most parts consists of these five parts; the second has four parts; the third, three; then there is one of two parts; which is in dispute.

And the rights of nature indeed are less inquired into for this controversy, because they are not engaged with this civil law and are rather remote from common understanding; but for some resemblance, or to amplify a matter, they are often to be introduced. But that is thought to be law by custom which the will of all, without a law, has approved through long usage. And in it some rights are already established on account of their antiquity. In which kind there are many other things, and much the greatest part of them is what the praetors have been accustomed to proclaim. And some kinds of law have already been made established by custom;

As to whether it can consist of even a single part, it may seem possible to someone. Of those, then, which are settled we shall set down examples; of those which are doubtful we shall bring forward reasons. The five-part argument is of this kind: "All laws, judges, ought to be referred to the advantage of the commonwealth, and they ought to be interpreted according to the common benefit, not according to the letter that is in the writing. For our ancestors were of such virtue and wisdom that, in writing the laws, they proposed to themselves nothing else but the safety and advantage of the commonwealth. For they did not themselves wish to write what would be harmful, and, if they had written it, they understood that, once it was perceived, the law would be repudiated. For no one wishes the laws to be preserved for the sake of the laws, but for the sake of the commonwealth, since all think the commonwealth best administered by the laws. Therefore, for the very reason that the laws ought to be observed, it is fitting that all that is written should be interpreted toward that end: that is, since we serve the commonwealth, let us interpret according to the advantage and benefit of the commonwealth. For as one ought to think that nothing proceeds from medicine except what looks to the advantage of the body, since for its sake it was established, so one should judge that nothing proceeds from the laws except what is conducive to the commonwealth, since for its sake they were framed.

of which kind are agreement, fairness, the adjudged. An agreement is what is settled between parties, and is thought so just that it is said to hold good by law; the fair is what is equitable toward all; the adjudged is that about which the opinion of someone or of several has already been established before. Now the rights established by statute must be learned from the laws. From these parts of law, then, whatever shall seem to arise for each side, either from the matter itself, or from a like, or from a greater or lesser, it will be necessary to attend to and to elicit by trying out each several part of law. But since, as was said before, there are two kinds of commonplaces, of which one contains the amplification of a doubtful matter, the other of a certain matter, it will be considered what the cause itself gives, and what can and ought to be amplified through a commonplace. For

Therefore in this trial too cease to scrutinize the letter of the law, and consider the law, as is just, according to the advantage of the commonwealth. What was more advantageous to the Thebans than that the Spartans should be crushed? For whom was it more fitting that Epaminondas, the general of the Thebans, should take thought than for the victory of the Thebans? What was it fitting for him to hold dearer or more precious than the great glory of the Thebans, than so bright and adorned a trophy? Was he, forsooth, to neglect the letter of the law and consider the framer's intent? But this surely has been sufficiently considered: that there is no law which has not been written for the sake of the commonwealth. He thought it, therefore, the greatest madness that what had been written for the sake of the safety of the commonwealth should not be interpreted according to the safety of the commonwealth. But if it is fitting that all laws be referred to the advantage of the commonwealth, and this man benefited the safety of the commonwealth, surely he cannot by the same deed both have looked to the common fortunes and have failed to obey the laws."

fixed topics, which fall upon all cases, cannot be prescribed; in most cases perhaps one will have to speak from the authority of the jurists and against their authority. But attention must be paid, both in this and in all cases, whether the matter itself shows any commonplaces besides those which we set forth. Now let us consider the juridical kind and its parts. The juridical is that in which the nature of the fair and the unfair, and the principle of reward or punishment, is inquired into. Its parts are two, of which we name the one absolute, the other assumptive. The absolute is that which contains in itself, not implicitly and hidden, as the negotial, but more openly and readily, the question of right and not-right. It is of this kind: when the Thebans had overcome the Spartans in war, and it was generally the custom of the Greeks, when they had waged war among themselves, that those who had conquered should set up some trophy in the territory, only for the sake of declaring the victory at the present moment, not that the memory of the war should remain forever, the Thebans set up a bronze trophy. They are accused before the Amphictyons. The charge is:

An argument consists of four parts when we either propose or assume without a proof. This one ought to do when either the proposition is understood of itself, or the assumption is evident and needs no proof. With the proof of the proposition passed over, the argument is handled in four parts, in this manner: "Judges, you who judge under oath according to the law, ought to obey the laws. But you cannot obey the laws unless you follow what is written in the law. For what surer testimony of his intent could the framer of the law leave than that which he himself wrote with great care and diligence? But if the writing did not exist, we should greatly require it, that from it the framer's intent might be known; nor yet would we permit Epaminondas, not even if he were outside the court, to interpret for us the intent of the law—much less now should we suffer this man, when the law is at hand, to interpret the framer's intent, not from what is written most plainly, but from what suits his own cause. But if you, judges, ought to obey the laws, and cannot do this unless you follow what is written in the law, why do you not judge that this man has acted against the law?"

"It was not fitting." The rebuttal is: "It was fitting." The question is: "Was it fitting?" The reason is: "For we won by valour such glory from the war that we wished to leave eternal tokens of it to our descendants." The invalidation is: "But nevertheless it is not fitting that Greeks should set up against Greeks an eternal monument of enmities." The point for decision is: "When the Greeks, for the sake of celebrating the highest valour, set up against Greeks an eternal monument of enmities, did they act rightly or the contrary?" We have subjoined this reason in order that the very kind of cause we are treating might be recognized. For if we had subjoined that which perhaps they used—"You waged the war neither justly nor dutifully"—we should slip into the retort of the charge, of which we shall speak later. But it is clear that both kinds of cause fall upon this case. For it the arguments must be taken from the same topics as in the negotial cause, of which we spoke before.

But with the proof of the assumption passed over, the four-part argument will be made thus: "Those who have time and again deceived us through trust ought not to have their word believed. For if we suffer any harm through their treachery, there will be no one but ourselves whom we can rightly accuse. And to be deceived once is unfortunate; a second time, foolish; a third time, disgraceful. But the Carthaginians have very often by now deceived us. It is therefore the greatest madness to place hope in the trustworthiness of those by whose treachery you have so often been deceived."

But it will be permitted and fitting to take commonplaces, both from the cause itself, if there shall be any matter of indignation or appeal to pity in it, and from the usefulness and nature of law—many and weighty ones—if the dignity of the cause shall seem to demand it. Now let us consider the assumptive part of the juridical. The assumptive, then, is said to be that when the deed itself cannot be approved of itself, but is defended by some argument joined from outside. Its parts are four: comparison, retort of the charge, shifting of the charge, and confession.

With both proofs passed over, it becomes three-part, in this way: "Either we must fear the Carthaginians, if we leave them unharmed, or we must destroy their city. But fear them indeed we ought not. It remains, then, that we destroy their city." There are, however, those who think that sometimes the conclusion can be dispensed with, when what is inferred from the reasoning is evident; and that, if this be done, the argument becomes two-part as well, in this manner: "If she has given birth, she is not a virgin; but she has given birth." Here it is enough to propose and to assume: since what is inferred is evident, the matter does not need a conclusion. But to us it seems that every reasoning ought to be concluded, and that the fault which displeases those men should be greatly avoided—namely, that we should not bring into the conclusion what is evident.

Comparison is when something done, which of itself is not to be approved, is defended from that for the sake of which it was done. It is of this kind: a certain general, when he was being besieged by the enemy and could in no way escape, made a bargain with them that he should leave his arms and baggage and lead out his soldiers; and so he did. With his arms and baggage lost, he saved his soldiers beyond hope.

And this can be done if the kinds of conclusions are understood.
